passage: At Gulab's tea stall in a small Bihar town, the argument had started over the morning paper. "Quotas kill merit!" said a man in a checked shirt, banging his glass. "My son studied day and night and missed the seat by two marks." "And my father cleaned classrooms so I could read," said Rehana, twenty-one, quietly. "I'm the first in my family in college." Voices rose. Rekha, twenty, felt the slogans pulling at her like a current, first one way, then the other. She wanted to shout along with someone. Instead she said, "Uncle, which exam was your son's? Rehana, will you show me the college's admission list?" Both looked surprised. Later, at the library, Rekha read the published figures beside Rehana's story. "It's more complicated than either slogan," she told Rehana.

qa.q: Where did the argument take place?
qa.a: The argument took place at Gulab's tea stall in a small Bihar town.

qa.q: What is Rekha feeling as the argument rises?
qa.a: Rekha feels pulled and restless. The slogans tug at her from both sides and she wants to shout along, but she holds back.

qa.q: What choice did Rekha make instead of joining a side?
qa.a: She asked questions of both speakers and later read the published figures next to Rehana's story, so her view could grow from lived experience and facts.

qa.q: How might the man in the checked shirt feel about his son's missing the seat?
qa.a: Probably hurt and worried for his son's future. His angry slogan may be covering a real disappointment, and Rekha's question about the exam lets him tell more.

grounding: A young adult hears heated quota arguments, feels drawn to slogans, and chooses to listen to lived experience and to data respectfully.

passage: In the student café in Porto, the debate about the university's new places for rural students had reached its third coffee. "It's not fair to city students," said Santiago, tapping the table. "I worked two jobs for my grades." "Two jobs is hard," answered Ines, "but my school had no chemistry teacher for a year." Emil, nineteen, sat between them with a half-eaten pastry. Emil felt the pull of both sides, and of the sharp lines friends kept posting online. Emil did not want a team. "Can I ask something?" Emil said. "Santiago, what would make it feel fair to you? Ines, what did the year without a teacher cost you?" They both slowed down. Afterwards Emil read the university's published report on who applied and who got in, and noted what it showed and what it left out.

qa.q: How long had Ines's school gone without a chemistry teacher?
qa.a: Ines's school had no chemistry teacher for a year.

qa.q: What is Emil feeling as Santiago and Ines argue?
qa.a: Emil feels pulled in both directions and reluctant to pick a side. Emil does not want a team.

qa.q: What choice did Emil make that changed the tone of the debate?
qa.a: Emil asked each of them a calm question about what would feel fair and what the year had cost, so they slowed down and explained instead of shouting.

qa.q: How might Santiago have felt after Emil's question?
qa.a: Possibly heard for the first time. Being asked what would feel fair, not just told to be quiet, may soften Santiago's anger.

grounding: A young adult hears heated arguments about quotas and merit, resists picking a tribe, and turns to listening and published data.

passage:
The hostel common room in Pune was packed the night the new admission list came out. Dhruv was standing on a chair, shouting a slogan about merit, and half the room was shouting back.
Lalremsiami, nineteen, sat near the door with her tea going cold. She felt the pull of it: the noise, the certainty, the easy side to join.
Then Sapna from her corridor, who rarely spoke, said quietly, "My father was the first in our village to finish school. People still call me 'quota' like it's my name." The shouting faltered.
Someone else said, "My cousin missed a seat by two marks. He was crushed." Both were true.
Lalremsiami didn't pick a slogan. She pulled up the official seat figures on her phone and asked, "Can we look at the numbers and then take turns?" Dhruv climbed down, grumbling, and sat.

qa.q: Who was standing on a chair shouting a slogan?
qa.a: Dhruv was standing on a chair, shouting a slogan about merit.

qa.q: What was Lalremsiami feeling as the argument grew?
qa.a: She felt drawn in by the noise and certainty, tempted to pick a side, but stayed thoughtful and held back.

qa.q: Which choice did Lalremsiami make, and why did it help the room?
qa.a: She listened to both people's lived experience, suggested looking at the official figures and taking turns, which kept the room respectful.

qa.q: How might Sapna feel when she speaks up?
qa.a: Sapna may feel nervous and exposed, sharing a painful experience of being called 'quota' in front of an angry room.

grounding: A young adult observing a heated quota debate feels the pull of slogans but chooses to listen to lived experience and data and keep things respectful.

passage:
Hi Lalit Mama,
You asked how college is. Honestly, the lectures are fine. It's the arguments that are exhausting.
Every week there's a new fight about reservations in our canteen. One side calls the other "anti-merit." The other side says "casteist." I've found myself nodding along to whoever is loudest, and last Thursday I almost shared an angry post I hadn't even read properly.
What stopped me was a conversation with my lab partner. He told me his grandmother wasn't allowed to draw water from the village well. And my roommate told me how her brother lost a seat by one rank and stopped eating for days. Both stories stayed with me.
So I've started doing something you'd like: I read the actual policy reports before I say anything, and I ask people what happened to them before I tell them what I think.
Is that too slow? It feels right.
Deepika

qa.q: What did Deepika almost share last Thursday?
qa.a: She almost shared an angry post she hadn't even read properly.

qa.q: How does Deepika feel about the weekly arguments?
qa.a: Deepika feels exhausted by them and uneasy about nodding along to whoever is loudest.

qa.q: Why is Deepika's new habit a wise one?
qa.a: Reading the policy reports and asking people about their experiences before giving an opinion helps Deepika understand both sides and stay respectful instead of joining a camp.

qa.q: How might Lalit Mama feel reading the letter?
qa.a: He would likely feel proud and reassured that Deepika is thinking carefully rather than following slogans.

grounding: A young adult who hears heated quota debates writes about feeling drawn to slogans and choosing lived experience and data instead.

passage:
Jaya, you asked why I quit the debate club's group chat. Okay, here's what happened.
In second year, the reservation topic came up and I was angry. My friend had missed a seat, and I had a slogan ready for every post. I felt powerful typing them.
Then our debate coach made us switch sides for a formal debate. I had to argue the other case. So I read. The historical exclusion. The data on who still gets hired. I interviewed our hostel mess manager, who told me what his school had been like.
And then I interviewed my friend who'd missed the seat, properly, not just to be angry for him.
I didn't come out with a neat answer. I came out knowing that both of them were real people, not sides. The group chat only wanted sides. So I left.
That's all it was, Jaya. Omkar listening, for once.

qa.q: Whom did Omkar interview first?
qa.a: He interviewed their hostel mess manager.

qa.q: How did Omkar feel when typing slogans in second year?
qa.a: Omkar felt angry and powerful, caught up in the heat of the argument.

qa.q: What was the turning point, and why did it help?
qa.a: Being made to argue the other side pushed Omkar to read data and interview real people on both sides, which replaced slogans with understanding.

qa.q: How might Omkar's friend have felt being interviewed properly?
qa.a: The friend may have felt listened to rather than used as a symbol, seen as a real person with a real disappointment.

grounding: A young adult who was pulled toward angry slogans in quota debates learns to listen to lived experience and data and stays respectful.

passage: My name is Arohi. In the canteen on Tuesday the quota argument started again, and I was halfway to joining it. Hemant stood on a bench with his fist up, repeating a line from some video: "Merit is dead!" A few people cheered. I felt the heat of it in my own chest; it is easy to want a side. Then Pallavi, usually quiet, said her mother was the first in their village to finish school, and a reserved seat had made the difference. Nobody cheered for that. Someone else opened the government's own admission figures on a phone, and the numbers were messier than either slogan. Hemant climbed down. I can't say what he was thinking; his jaw was tight. I bought two teas and asked Pallavi to tell me more.

qa.q: What line was Hemant repeating on the bench?
qa.a: He was repeating "Merit is dead!"

qa.q: What was Arohi feeling as the canteen cheered, and how can you tell?
qa.a: Arohi felt a hot pull of excitement and anger, the heat in the chest that makes picking a side tempting.

qa.q: What did Arohi do that was wiser than joining a side?
qa.a: Arohi listened to Pallavi's lived story, noticed the real figures were messier than the slogans, and chose to keep asking questions over tea.

qa.q: How might Pallavi have experienced the canteen argument?
qa.a: Pallavi might have felt her family's real life was being turned into a slogan, and speaking quietly about her mother took some courage.

grounding: It illustrates a young adult drawn toward angry slogans in a quota debate who instead listens to lived experience and to data while staying respectful.
